one_liner: TensorFlow Lite custom ops for binarized neural networks on 64-bit ARM; reports lower Bi-RealNet latency than dabnn on a Pixel 1.
what_it_does: Runs binarized neural networks (1-bit weights and activations, as trained with Larq) on mobile and embedded CPUs. A Python converter (pip package larq-compute-engine, MLIR-based) turns a Larq/Keras model into a .tflite flatbuffer and replaces the emulated binary layers with LCE custom ops (LceBconv2d, LceBMaxPool2d, LceQuantize, LceDequantize). At runtime you build a standard TFLite interpreter and register the LCE ops alongside the built-in ones, so non-binary layers still run on stock TFLite and XNNPACK. It is not a drop-in replacement for any library: you need a model trained for binarization.
how_it_is_fast: Binary convolution becomes a binary GEMM: activations and weights are bit-packed into 32-bit words, and each multiply-accumulate is an XOR followed by a popcount. On AArch64 the indirect-BGEMM kernels (8x4x1, 8x4x2 and 8x4x4, picked at runtime from the packed input depth) do this in inline NEON assembly (eor, cnt, addp) with 16-bit accumulators, and the im2col path plugs custom kernels into Google's Ruy GEMM framework. The kernels apply a per-channel output transform (multiplier, bias, clamp) in the same pass, and since v0.7.0 the converter keeps activations bit-packed between binary layers by default.
when_to_use: You are deploying a BNN (QuickNet, Bi-RealNet or your own Larq model) to an AArch64 phone or board such as Android or Raspberry Pi 4 in 64-bit mode.
Your binary layers are standard 2D convolutions (grouped convolutions are supported since v0.5/v0.6) and the rest of the model can stay on built-in TFLite ops.
You already train with Larq/Keras and want a converter path that keeps the training graph and the deployed graph consistent.
You want per-layer latency numbers on device: the repo ships a TFLite benchmark tool with the LCE ops registered.
when_not_to_use: Full-precision or int8 models: LCE adds nothing; it only speeds up layers that are truly binarized, and binarization costs accuracy (QuickNet tops out at 66.9% ImageNet top-1).
x86 or other non-AArch64 targets as an inference engine: the hand-written kernels are AArch64-only, and elsewhere the code falls back to portable C++ (Ruy kStandardCpp path, std::bitset popcount).
GPUs, NPUs or LLM workloads: CPU only, convnet-oriented ops.
Projects that cannot take a Bazel build pinned to a specific TensorFlow source tree (TF 2.16.1 in WORKSPACE, Bazel 6.5.0).
Teams wanting fast upstream movement: the last tagged release is v0.16.0 (2024-06-21) and recent commits are mostly dependency bumps.

integration.form: static lib (TFLite custom-op library built with Bazel against a pinned TensorFlow source tree) plus a Python converter wheel
integration.dependencies: TensorFlow Lite (TensorFlow 2.16.1 sources), Ruy, flatbuffers; the converter needs Python 3.10-3.12 and TensorFlow >= 2.8; Bazel 6.5.0 to build
integration.min_toolchain: Bazel 6.5.0; aarch64 builds use -march=armv8-a; Android NDK for Android; exact minimum compiler not documented
integration.platforms: Optimized kernels: AArch64 (Android, 64-bit Raspberry Pi and other ARM boards, Apple M1 per the README benchmarks). Portable C++ fallback elsewhere. Converter wheels: Linux x86-64, macOS x86-64 and arm64, Windows x86-64.
integration.thread_safety: Not documented beyond TFLite interpreter rules (one interpreter per thread; intra-op threads via TFLite's thread count). Issue #730 (2022) reported the aarch64 benchmark tool crashing with --num_threads=2 on Raspberry Pi and Jetson; closed a day later, resolution not visible on the page.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — the model must be trained with Larq and converted with the LCE converter; the TFLite interpreter API is unchanged, you only register the extra custom ops

gotchas: Kernels may read (never write) up to 16 bytes past the end of an array (LCE_EXTRA_BYTES in core/types.h); custom tensor allocations need that padding.

The AArch64 assembly kernels use 16-bit accumulators and are chosen only if the maximum accumulator value fits in uint16; otherwise the code falls back to the portable 4x2 C++ kernel, and bit-packed output is also portable-only.
The benchmark tool defaults to use_indirect_bgemm=false (Ruy-based BGEMM); pass the flag to measure the indirect kernels.
Open bug #421 (since 2020): int8 default ranges break when a binary conv is followed by a normal conv.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick LCE over MNN, OpenVINO or FeatherCNN only when your network is binarized end to end, since those engines target float/int8 models; pick BitNet (bitnet.cpp) or T-MAC instead for low-bit LLM inference, which is where LCE has no kernels.
verified_claims_summary: The README reports first-party latencies from its TFLite benchmark tool with XNNPACK enabled and random inputs: Bi-RealNet runs in 41.6 ms on a Pixel 1, versus the 61.3 ms that dabnn published for the same model (about 1.47x, a cross-report comparison, not a same-run measurement); QuickNet runs in 25.5 ms single-threaded on a Pixel 1 and 45.0 ms on a Raspberry Pi 4B. The MLSys 2021 paper's 8.5-18.5x figure (known only from search snippets) compares binary convolutions with full-precision ones, which is not equal work; no compiler flags are stated.
status_note: Apache-2.0 and still receiving commits (mostly dependency bumps, plus a RISC-V build path in 2026), but the last PyPI release is v0.16.0 from June 2024 and the build is tied to TensorFlow 2.16.1, so expect to do your own porting.
